title: Surdas's single line
hook: a single line: leave the company of those turned away from the Lord (Sarang, Surdas, ang 1253)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Parmanand asked what all the listening was for. Your line was hear, then do. Did one story you'd heard turn into one thing you did? Day seven hundred eighty-eight.

Some parts of the Guru Granth Sahib run on for pages: long ballads, rows and rows of saloks. And then, in Raag Sarang, on the same Ang as yesterday's hymn, there's the name Surdas, and with it a single line. That's it. No verses after it, no story around it. It sits there like a note pinned to a door on the way out. Somebody decided one line was worth keeping, and it carries Surdas's name.
screen: `PAGES OF BALLADS AND SALOKS.` → `A HEADING: SURDAS.` → `ONE LINE, PINNED TO THE DOOR.`

segments.voice: Here is the line, in paraphrase: O mind, leave the company of those who have turned away from the Lord. The key word is bemukh: one whose face is turned the other way. Not a bad person in a cartoon sense. Someone whose face is pointed elsewhere, whose whole attention is turned away from God. Who was this Surdas? Tradition tells more than one story about the name, and the Granth itself doesn't settle it. What it gives is the line, and where it puts the line. Just before it stands a hymn headed with Guru Arjan's mark and the name Surdas together, about the Lord's people who live close to the Lord. So on one page you get both sides of the same idea: the company that draws you near, and the company that turns you away. Now the hard part, because a line like this can be misused. It isn't a license to look down on anyone. Sikh teaching puts great weight on sangat, the company you keep, because company shapes a mind the way water shapes a stone, slowly and without asking. The line talks to the mind, not to the neighbors. It doesn't say: judge them. It says: notice what you're sitting in. A mind spends its days somewhere. With people, with voices, with feeds and habits. Some of that company turns the face toward what matters. Some turns it away a little more each day, so slowly it's easy to miss. Surdas doesn't argue the case. He doesn't need to. One line, and the choosing is left to you.
screen: `O MIND, LEAVE THE COMPANY OF THE TURNED-AWAY.` · `BIMUKH: THE FACE TURNED THE OTHER WAY.` · `TWO SIDES ON ONE PAGE.` · `SANGAT SHAPES A MIND, NOT A LICENSE TO JUDGE.` · then, large: `ONE LINE.`

segments.voice: Today's practice: choose your company. In the sit, let the last few days pass in front of you. The people you spent time with. The voices in your ears, the screens, the conversations. Don't judge anyone. Just notice which ones left your face turned toward what you care about, and which ones turned it away. Then pick one good company, a person, a place, a sound, and decide to give it a little more of your time this week. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Bemukh. One whose face is turned away from the Lord: Surdas's single line, kept whole, telling the mind to leave that company.
Your line: one line. Today, give one hour to company that turns your face the right way, and notice how the mind feels after. Day seven hundred eighty-eight.

howItsDone: Sikhs speak of sangat, the company of those who remember God, as something that shapes a person, and gather in the gurdwara partly to keep that company; Surdas's line is read in that light.

original.note: Gurmukhi: with the face turned away; the word at the heart of Surdas's line.

what it means: O mind, leave the company of those whose faces are turned from the Lord; the line is about what shapes your own mind.
what a scholar hears: one line under Surdas's name, set just after a hymn headed with Guru Arjan's mark and Surdas's name, so the page holds both kinds of company.

notes: Paraphrase of the line (chhaadi man har bimukhan ko sang): confirm.
Hymn headed 'Sarang Mahala 5 Surdas' just before the line, described as about the Lord's people dwelling with the Lord (har ke sang base har lok): confirm placement and description.
'Tradition tells more than one story about the name': deliberately avoids identifying this Surdas with the blind Krishna poet; confirm a Keeper is comfortable with this.
